opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest challenge is that the models are very good at producing text that looks like fiction, but not so good at producing fiction that actually has something to say. If you just ask a model to "write a chapter," you get something fluent, grammatically perfect, with all the right genre beats, and it's completely flat. It reads like the average of every novel it has seen. And in a way that's exactly what it is, because the training objective pulls it toward the most likely continuation, and good fiction is almost by definition not the most likely continuation. The surprising twist, the odd detail, the character who does something you didn't expect but that in hindsight feels inevitable: that's the opposite of what a next-token predictor naturally gravitates to.

The second challenge is long-range structure. When I write, I usually have the whole arc in my head: what each character knows, what they're hiding, what the reader should suspect by chapter five but not confirm until chapter twelve. Current models can hold a lot of context, but holding text is different from holding intention. They'll forget that a character was supposed to be lying, or they'll resolve a tension too early because resolving things feels "helpful." Planting foreshadowing and keeping a secret for three hundred pages is a planning problem, not a writing problem, and the models aren't really planning in that sense.

So in practice, what works for me is using AI more as a sparring partner than a ghostwriter. I'll ask it to brainstorm ten ways a scene could go, and usually nine are clichés, but the act of seeing the clichés laid out helps me find the tenth option that's actually interesting. Or I'll use it to check consistency, like "does this character's behavior here contradict what they said earlier?" That's genuinely useful. But the core of it, deciding what the story means and why anyone should care, still has to come from the human. And honestly, as a researcher, I find that gap really interesting, because it tells you something about what these models are still missing: not language ability, but something closer to taste and long-horizon intent.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI fiction as flat, generic, and cliché-prone, but does not identify removing the AI’s characteristic stylistic flavor as a challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the core challenge is that fiction is the opposite of what these models are naturally good at.

Language models are trained to predict the most likely next token. That makes them excellent at producing text that reads as fluent, plausible, and average. But good fiction lives in the surprising choice, the detail that is specific rather than typical. When I ask a model to write a scene, the first draft tends to be smooth and completely forgettable. Every character speaks a bit like a corporate memo. Every emotion is named rather than shown. The model gives you the center of the distribution, and literature is mostly about the tails.

The second challenge is long-range consistency. A novel is a hundred thousand words where a detail planted in chapter two has to pay off in chapter thirty. Models have gotten much better with longer context, but keeping a character's voice, motivations, and small physical facts coherent across that span is still hard. You end up acting as the continuity editor, which is tedious work.

The third one is more personal. I've been writing fiction as a hobby, and I've found that the moment the AI starts generating prose for me, I lose something. The reason I write is to find out what I actually think, and that only happens through the friction of choosing each sentence myself. So the way I use these tools has shifted. I use them as a sparring partner. I'll ask, give me ten possible endings for this scene, and nine of them will be bad, but one will push me to think about a direction I hadn't considered. Or I'll describe a plot problem and have it argue with me. That's genuinely useful.

So the challenge isn't really whether AI can write fiction. It's figuring out how to use a system that is optimized for the probable to help you discover the improbable, without letting it flatten your own voice in the process.

r001.rationale: The response identifies the model’s fluent, average, forgettable prose as a challenge for fiction, and explains that fiction needs surprising, specific choices to counter that style.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenge is maintaining a coherent vision over a long story. AI can help you write a paragraph or brainstorm what happens next, but a novel requires more than locally plausible text. A character has motivations, those motivations shape their decisions, and those decisions have consequences many chapters later. You need all of that to hold together.

There’s also the question of what you actually want to say. If you ask AI to make a scene more dramatic, it can add a conflict or a surprise. But does that serve the story? Does it reveal something about the character? You still need to make those judgments. So I see AI as a useful partner for exploring possibilities, while the writer provides the direction and decides which possibilities matter.

r001.rationale: The response discusses maintaining story coherence and choosing meaningful creative direction, but does not identify removing AI’s characteristic stylistic flavor as a challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the challenge is that writing fiction is not just about generating fluent sentences. You need an overall vision: what the characters want, why they make certain choices, and how those choices lead to an ending. AI can give you something that sounds quite reasonable locally, but over a whole story, it may lose that thread.

And sometimes you don’t know exactly what you want until you start writing. You discover the story in the process. So the interesting question is how AI can help you explore possibilities while still letting you develop your own voice and judgment. It’s easy to produce more text; it’s much harder to produce a story you actually care about.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions preserving the writer’s own voice, but does not identify removing AI’s characteristic stylistic flavor as a challenge.
